decks.domain: Driving basics and sharing the road

cards.front: How should you set up the car before starting the engine?
cards.back: Start per the owner manual with the parking brake set, a stick shift out of gear with clutch down as needed, and an automatic selector in park.

cards.front: How should you feed in speed, and why practice the clutch and throttle?
cards.back: Feed speed in gently since hard launches spin wheels and slide cars, and rehearse clutch and throttle so shifts neither race nor stall.

cards.front: Where do your hands go on the wheel, and how do you steer through sharp bends?
cards.back: Grip the wheel at eight to ten left and two to four right, hand over hand through sharp bends while straightening manually, or push pull with outward knuckles and uncrossed hands.

cards.front: Where and how far ahead should your eyes scan, and how do you time it?
cards.back: Scan ahead, aside and astern always, holding eyes twelve seconds out, about a city block downtown or four blocks on highways, timed by counting thousands to a fixed object.

cards.front: When should you favor side glances, and when should you favor rear checks?
cards.back: Favor side glances at crossings and lane moves and rear checks in dense traffic, lane shifts, slowdowns, reversing and long descents.

cards.front: How do you check that you are not driving faster than you can see?
cards.back: Never outdrive vision: pick a far fixed mark and if it arrives before four counted thousands, shed speed at once.

cards.front: How does the look ahead habit differ from the separate sight rule for speed?
cards.back: Safe eyes ride twelve seconds ahead, one block in town or four on highways, while the separate four second sight rule caps speed against visible distance.

decks.domain: Driving basics and sharing the road

cards.front: What must you do before entering a crossing, turning left, or turning right?
cards.back: Enter crossings only after left right scans, cede left turns to all oncoming traffic including bikes while rechecking twice, and turn right solely past clear lefts, clear paths, patient bikes and legal reds.

cards.front: How should you treat traffic signals, blind corners and a crowded intersection?
cards.back: Trust no signal blindly, scan even fresh greens, halt for dead lights as for stop signs, creep out past blind corners, and never strand the car blocking the box.

cards.front: What must you do at a railroad crossing, especially with more than one track?
cards.back: Slow and sweep both rail directions at every crossing with far side room assured, and past multi track trains linger until the first clears sight of a second.

cards.front: How do left turn yields differ from a right turn on red?
cards.back: Left turns bow to every oncoming vehicle and bike with double rechecks, whereas right turns on red need only a full stop, clear lefts and paths, and no banning sign.

cards.front: What does a dead signal become, and what does a fresh green still demand?
cards.back: A dead signal legally becomes a stop sign for all, yet even a live fresh green still demands left right scans for red runners.

cards.front: When must you wait to enter, and when may you edge forward slowly?
cards.back: Heavy traffic forbids entering without far side room to dodge gridlock, but a blind corner invites a slow edge forward so cross traffic spots the nose first.

decks.domain: Driving basics and sharing the road

cards.front: How do work zones warn drivers, and which speed limits apply there?
cards.back: Work zones speak through orange and black roadside boards on the right, or both sides when divided, and post lower limits that rule unless absent.

cards.front: What can work zone violations cost, and what happens to handheld phone fines?
cards.back: Zone speeding, disobedience, lane abuse or worker endangerment can cost a thousand dollars plus points and retraining, with handheld phone fines doubled inside.

cards.front: How should you drive through a work zone, including at night?
cards.back: Through zones slow down, heed boards and flaggers, respect shifting lanes, and drive nights with extreme care whether crews show or not.

cards.front: Which other habits does the manual list for work zones?
cards.back: Also watch brake lights ahead, merge early, slide from workers, shun tailgates, honor mobile crews to the End Road Work board, drop distractions, detour when able, and bank extra time calmly.

decks.domain: Driving basics and sharing the road

cards.front: Who is protected by stiffer penalties for careless harm, and how much room must every pass leave?
cards.back: Careless harm to walkers, riders, wheelchair users, animal traffic, road crews, garbage, tank, mail and express haulers draws stiffer penalties, and every pass must leave three feet.

cards.front: What must you do for sirens and flashers, and for any roadside stop?
cards.back: Sirens and red or blue flashers command a right edge stop held until passage unless officers wave on, while any roadside stop demands slowing below the limit plus one lane over when safe.

cards.front: When does a walker own a crosswalk, and what must doors never strike?
cards.back: Walkers own every crosswalk, painted or sidewalk implied, once a raised hand or any body part or aid enters its mouth, and doors must never strike people, bikes or traffic.

cards.front: Which rule do painted crosswalks and sidewalk extensions share?
cards.back: Painted crosswalks and invisible sidewalk extensions share one rule: raised hands or entering limbs and aids all claim the right of way.

cards.front: Who always wins the right of way with a held full stop, even on a green?
cards.back: White canes and guide dogs always win the right of way with full stops held until the road clears, greens notwithstanding at regulated corners.

cards.front: How do ordinary walkers' rights differ from those of cane and guide dog users?
cards.back: Ordinary walkers win crossings on intent, while cane and guide dog users win absolute held stops that outlast even green lights.

cards.front: Where must you guard hardest for children, and what must you obey and halt for?
cards.back: Guard hardest for children near schools, stops, parks and ice cream trucks plus every driveway reversal, obey posted school limits, and halt for crossing pupils and guard signals.

cards.front: What must you do near a lit ice cream truck with its arms out?
cards.back: Lit ice cream trucks with arms out force a ten foot stop fore or aft, then five mile per hour creeping yielded to crossing children, except across islands or barriers.

decks.domain: Driving basics and sharing the road

cards.front: How does the manual treat bikes, and which riders deserve widened caution?
cards.back: Bikes count as vehicles owning lanes outright when narrow, while unskilled wobblers ignoring signs and night lights deserve widened caution.

cards.front: What does the manual list as duties for bike riders?
cards.back: Riders keep right as safe, may hold a right turn lane left edge going straight, obey signs with hand signals, yield to walkers, helmet under sixteen, and dress bright with lights and tuned machines.

cards.front: When must drivers yield to bikes, and how should they pass them?
cards.back: Drivers yield to bikes at crossings, paths and pre turn cuts under doubled failure fines, pass slow with three feet minding width and loads, then avoid quick slows, stops and right hooks plus needless horn blasts.

cards.front: What must turning drivers watch for, and where may they pass a bike?
cards.back: Turning drivers hunt for bikes and sidewalk children, never slice or shoulder riders off, expect wrong way wheels and sloppy wet handling, may pass safely inside no passing zones, and keep bike lanes, doors and reverse paths bike checked.

cards.front: What do bike passes need, and how do bike yield fines differ from ordinary ones?
cards.back: Bike passes need three feet of air with slow care, and skipping a bike yield costs doubled fines unlike ordinary yield slips.

cards.front: Where may a slow bike be passed, and what do bike lanes forbid?
cards.back: Slow bikes may be passed inside no passing zones when sight allows, yet bike lanes themselves forbid driving, parking and stopping except crossings and emergencies.
cards.memory_hook: pass by sight, lanes off limits

decks.domain: Driving basics and sharing the road

cards.front: What lane rights and blind spot risks does the manual give motorcycles, and why hunt for them on left turns?
cards.back: Bikes own full lanes sharable by pairs only, hide in blind spots needing head turns, and die mostly when cars left hook them, so left turns demand motorcycle hunts.

cards.front: How should you signal, follow and behave near a motorcycle?
cards.back: Distrust lingering bike blinkers, telegraph every move, gift room for pothole dodges, trail three to four seconds or longer when wet, dip beams, and hold course while being passed.

cards.front: Who may share a lane with a motorcycle, and who may not?
cards.back: Cars must never split a lane with a motorcycle, though two motorcycles themselves may legally share one lane side by side.

cards.front: What should you expect and grant to slow trucks, tractors, buses and triangle rigs?
cards.back: Expect sluggish trucks and tractors on grades, yield to signaling buses, grant orange triangle rigs under twenty five miles per hour room, and pass slow traffic lawfully even over double yellow with clear sight.

cards.front: How do horses travel, and how must drivers pass them?
cards.back: Horses travel single file rightward, and drivers must slow or halt with gentle space and silence, never horns or startling din.

decks.domain: Driving basics and sharing the road

cards.front: What happens in a big rig's side blind zones and behind it, and what gap should you hold?
cards.back: Big rig side blind zones swallow cars unseen in driver mirrors, and tailgating their rears blinds both parties to forward trouble, so hold real following gaps.

cards.front: Why must you not cut in front of a big rig, and where are its blind areas in turns?
cards.back: Sixty five foot rigs stopping on doubled room punish cut ins, so reenter only past full fronts in mirrors without slowing, and never wedge beside wide swinging turns blind twenty feet fore and two hundred aft.

cards.front: What are the limits of trucks, and which zones must every driver shun?
cards.back: Trucks crawl uphill, swing wide, brake long and tip tall, so human error by car drivers can still wreck the evading trucker: shun every No-Zone.

cards.front: How should you pass a truck?
cards.back: Pass trucks solely with room sans speeding, checked mirrors, legal ground, brisk cab clearance, mirror confirmed reentry right, and sustained pace after.

cards.front: How do the front and rear No-Zones differ?
cards.back: Front No-Zones punish early cut ins before whole fronts show in mirrors, while rear No-Zones punish tailgating that blinds both drivers forward.

recap_hooks.text: Set the parking brake and the right gear before starting, then feed speed in gently.
Keep the eyes twelve seconds ahead, and if a fixed mark arrives before four counted thousands, slow down at once.
Scan left and right before every crossing, and on a left turn yield to all oncoming traffic, bikes included.
Treat a dead signal as a stop sign, scan even on a fresh green, and never block the box.
At rail crossings, sweep both ways and wait until the first train clears your sight of a second.
Orange and black boards mark work zones, and their lower posted limits rule.
Zone violations can cost a thousand dollars plus points and retraining, and handheld phone fines double inside.
Slow down, heed flaggers, merge early and drive nights with extreme care.
Pull to the right edge for sirens and flashers, and move a lane over for roadside stops when safe.
A walker owns the crosswalk once a hand, body part or aid enters it, and white cane or guide dog users win even on a green.
Near a lit ice cream truck with its arms out, stop ten feet away, then creep at five miles per hour while yielding to crossing children.
Bikes count as vehicles, and riders keep right and wear helmets under sixteen.
Yield to bikes, pass slowly with three feet of room, and remember a missed bike yield doubles the fine.
A slow bike may be passed in a no passing zone when sight allows, but bike lanes stay off limits.
Never split a lane with a motorcycle, though two motorcycles may share one.
Trail a motorcycle three to four seconds or longer when wet, and hunt for motorcycles on left turns.
Give slow vehicles and horses room, and never sound a horn near horses.
A truck has side, front and rear No-Zones, so shun them: no early cut ins and no tailgating.
Pass a truck briskly with room, and reenter only when its full front shows in your mirror.
